title: MANNA GOT ITS NAME BECAUSE PEOPLE LOOKED AT GOD’S MIRACLE AND ASKED, “WHAT IS THIS?”
paragraphs: MANNA GOT ITS NAME BECAUSE PEOPLE LOOKED AT GOD’S MIRACLE AND ASKED, “WHAT IS THIS?”

They were starving. They were complaining. They were beginning to believe God had abandoned them. Then heaven covered the ground with something nobody could explain. But the greatest revelation wasn't what fell from heaven. It was Who would one day come down from heaven to save them.
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning with no food in your kitchen.
Not a single grain of rice. Not a piece of bread. Nothing in the refrigerator. No money to buy groceries. No guarantee that tomorrow will be any different.
Now imagine your children looking at you, asking when they are going to eat.
And you have no answer.
You try to be strong. You tell them everything will be okay. You smile because you don't want them to see how frightened you are.
But when everybody is asleep, you sit alone, staring at the ceiling, wondering how much longer you can survive.
You've prayed.
You've cried.
You've asked God to make a way.
And the silence feels unbearable.
Now imagine stepping outside the following morning and discovering that the ground is covered with something you've never seen before.
Something you didn't plant.
Something you couldn't manufacture.
Something you couldn't possibly have earned.
And all you can say is...
"What is this?"
That is almost exactly what happened to the Israelites in Exodus 16.
And here's the astonishing part.
The food God provided became known by a name connected to their bewildered question.
They didn't immediately recognize their miracle.
They had to ask what they were looking at.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to reach into your life.
Because sometimes the provision of God doesn't look anything like the answer you were expecting.
Sometimes the thing you've been praying for arrives so differently that you almost walk past it.
And sometimes God gives you exactly what you need while you're still struggling to believe He cares.
But to understand how extraordinary the manna really was, we need to return to the wilderness.
Not the beautiful wilderness in photographs.
The real wilderness.
The kind that makes people desperate.
The kind that exposes what is hiding inside the human heart.
The kind where faith is no longer something you merely talk about on Sunday.
It becomes a question of whether you will trust God when everything around you suggests you shouldn't.
The Israelites had recently witnessed one of the greatest acts of deliverance recorded in Scripture.
God had brought them out of Egypt.
They had seen His power over Pharaoh. They had crossed the sea on dry ground. They had watched the waters close over the pursuing Egyptian forces.
They had sung about God's victory.
They had celebrated their freedom.
But freedom didn't immediately mean comfort.
The road from slavery to the Promised Land passed through a wilderness.
And hunger has a terrible way of making yesterday's miracles feel distant.
Exodus 16:2–3 tells us that the congregation began grumbling against Moses and Aaron.
Their complaint was devastating.
They said they wished they had died in Egypt, where they remembered sitting beside pots of meat and eating bread until they were full.
Think about that.
They had escaped slavery, yet hunger made their former captivity appear desirable.
The same Egypt that had oppressed them was beginning to look like a place of security.
Their memories had become selective.
They remembered the food.
But their complaint pushed the suffering of slavery into the background.
And before we condemn them, we should recognize how easily the human heart does the same thing.
Have you ever begged God to deliver you from something, only to find yourself missing parts of it when following Him became difficult?
A relationship you knew was destroying your peace.
A habit you prayed for the strength to leave.
A lifestyle that kept pulling you farther from Christ.
An old identity that felt familiar even though it was slowly crushing you.
You knew you needed freedom.
But freedom demanded trust.
And trust felt frightening.
So you started remembering Egypt as though it had been paradise.
That is one of the dangers of spiritual exhaustion.
When the wilderness becomes painful enough, bondage can begin to look like provision.
But watch what God does next.
He doesn't announce that Israel has earned His kindness.
He doesn't pretend their grumbling is righteous.
He tells Moses that He will rain bread from heaven for them.
Exodus 16:4 records the Lord saying:
"Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you."
And the people would gather a daily portion, with God's instructions serving as a test of whether they would walk in His law.
There is a breathtaking tension here.
The people are complaining.
God is providing.
Their hearts are wavering.
His faithfulness is not.
This doesn't mean God approves of unbelief or rebellion. Scripture takes both seriously.
It means His covenant faithfulness is greater than the worthiness of the people He has chosen to lead.
And that distinction matters.
Because if every blessing depended upon our having a perfect day of faith, who among us could stand?
The wilderness was not simply a place where Israel needed food.
It was a place where Israel needed to learn who God was.
Then came the morning that would give the bread its unforgettable name.
Exodus 16:13–14 describes quail arriving in the evening and dew covering the camp in the morning.
When the dew lifted, something fine and flaky appeared on the wilderness surface, resembling frost.
Imagine thousands of people stepping out of their tents.
Children pointing.
Parents bending down.
Neighbors calling to one another.
Everyone staring at the strange substance covering the ground.
Nobody had planted it.
Nobody had baked it.
Nobody had carried it out of Egypt.
Then came the question.
Exodus 16:15 preserves the moment in Hebrew:
מָן הוּא
Man hu.
Commonly understood in the passage as:
"What is it?"
The verse explains that the Israelites spoke this way because they did not know what the substance was.
Moses then told them:
"It is the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat."
That wording comes from the King James Version of Exodus 16:15.
And the linguistic detail is fascinating.
The Hebrew word for manna is:
מָן — man
The narrative connects this name with the people's question, man hu.
Exodus 16:31 later says that the house of Israel called its name manna.
In Hebrew, the expression appears as:
מָן הוּא
The traditional explanation is that the name arose from the people's question, "What is it?"

There is a linguistic nuance worth preserving: the ordinary Biblical Hebrew expression for "what is it?" would more typically use mah for "what." Scholars have discussed the precise linguistic background of man, including the possibility of an older or related Semitic usage.
So the safest and most faithful way to state the discovery is this:
Exodus itself connects the name manna with Israel's bewildered question about the mysterious food God had provided.
That is what makes the story remarkable.
The Israelites didn't begin with an explanation.
They began with astonishment.
They were looking at God's provision before they understood what it was.
And Moses had to tell them what they were seeing.
"It is the bread which the LORD hath given you to eat."
Read that again.
Not bread they deserved.
Not bread they had manufactured.
Not bread they had purchased.
Bread the Lord had given.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something similar today.
You may be so focused on the form you expected God's help to take that you're struggling to recognize the help already in front of you.
Maybe you expected a dramatic breakthrough, but God is sustaining you through an ordinary job.
Maybe you expected immediate relief, but He is teaching you to endure through the support of faithful people.
Maybe you expected every problem to disappear, but He has given you strength to face another day.
We must be careful not to label every circumstance as a miraculous sign or promise that every hardship will quickly end.
But we should also be careful not to despise ordinary mercies simply because they arrive without thunder.
Not every provision announces itself with spectacle.
Sometimes it arrives quietly.
And gratitude begins when we recognize that everything good ultimately comes from God.
But the manna story becomes even more challenging.
Because God didn't simply give Israel food.
He gave them instructions about how to receive it.
They were to gather what they needed.
Each person was to receive an appropriate portion.
And ordinarily, they were not to keep the manna overnight.
Some people disobeyed.
They tried to preserve more than God had instructed.
By morning, the leftovers bred worms and stank.
Imagine the smell.
Imagine the disappointment.
Imagine discovering that the thing you desperately wanted to preserve had become rotten in your hands.
The problem wasn't that planning ahead is always wrong.
Scripture elsewhere commends wisdom, diligence, and responsible preparation.
The issue here was specific.
God had commanded Israel to gather the manna according to His instructions, and some refused to trust Him enough to obey.
They wanted tomorrow's security on their own terms.
And suddenly the wilderness story becomes painfully personal.
How many times have we done the same?
God calls us to obedience today.
But we want guarantees about next year.
God calls us to trust His character.
But we demand control over every outcome.
God calls us to follow Him.
But we keep negotiating because surrender feels too dangerous.
We want the blessing.
We want the provision.
We want the peace.
But we struggle with the daily dependence.
And perhaps that is why Jesus later taught His disciples to pray:
"Give us this day our daily bread."
Matthew 6:11.
Not because responsible planning is sinful.
Not because believers should never save money or prepare for the future.
But because even the most carefully planned life remains dependent upon God.
You can fill your cupboards and still have an empty soul.
You can build financial security and still be terrified of tomorrow.
You can have everything the world calls success and still lie awake wondering whether your life means anything.
There are hungers that food cannot satisfy.
And this is where the story begins moving toward something far greater than bread on the ground.
Because the manna was never meant to be the final answer to humanity's deepest need.
It sustained physical life for a time.
But it could not conquer death.
It could fill an empty stomach.
But it could not cleanse a guilty conscience.
It could help a generation survive the wilderness.
But it could not, by itself, reconcile sinners to a holy God.
For that, humanity needed something greater.
Someone greater.
And centuries later, Jesus Christ stood before a crowd that knew the story of Moses and the manna.
In John 6, Jesus had fed thousands with five barley loaves and two fish.
The crowd had witnessed extraordinary provision.
But Jesus exposed the deeper issue.
They were seeking Him because they had eaten the loaves and were filled.
Then the conversation turned toward the bread from heaven.
The people referred to the manna their ancestors had eaten in the wilderness.
And Jesus made a declaration that transformed the entire conversation.
In John 6:32–33, He explained that it was His Father who gives the true bread from heaven, and that the bread of God comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.
Then, in John 6:35, Jesus said:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς
Egō eimi ho artos tēs zōēs.
"I am the bread of life."
Those are the Greek words recorded in John's Gospel.
Egō eimi means "I am."
Ho artos means "the bread."
Tēs zōēs means "of life."
Jesus was not merely offering another meal.
He was identifying Himself as the One who satisfies the deepest spiritual need of those who come to Him in faith.
He continued:
"He that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst."
John 6:35, KJV.
Notice what Jesus didn't say.
He didn't say, "I will show you where to buy the bread of life."
He didn't say, "I will teach you how to manufacture the bread of life."
He said:
"I am the bread of life."
The provision was not merely something He carried.
The life He offered was found in Him.
And this is where the manna in Exodus becomes a breathtaking witness to the Gospel.
Israel needed bread to live in the wilderness.
Humanity needs Christ for eternal life.
The manna came down from heaven as God's provision for Israel.
Jesus declared that He had come down from heaven to do the Father's will.
The manna sustained people who would eventually die.
Jesus gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
Jesus Himself makes this contrast in John 6:49–51.
He says that the fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died, but He is the living bread that came down from heaven.
This isn't a connection we have to invent to make the story sound inspirational.
Jesus Himself draws the connection.
And He takes it further.
He speaks of giving His flesh for the life of the world.
The conversation points toward the astonishing cost of our redemption.
The Son of God did not enter the world merely to improve our circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
To bear our sins.
To give His life.
To rise again.
To bring those who trust in Him into fellowship with God.
The bread in the wilderness kept Israel alive for another day.
The Bread of Life gave Himself so that sinners could receive everlasting life.
And now I want you to consider something deeply personal.
What have you been feeding your soul lately?
Not your body.
Your soul.
Because people can spend their entire lives trying to satisfy spiritual hunger with things that were never designed to carry the weight of eternity.
Some feed their souls with approval.
They need to be admired, noticed, affirmed, and constantly reassured that they matter.
Others feed themselves with achievement.
Another promotion.
Another milestone.
Another accomplishment.
Another moment of recognition.
Others try to silence their hunger through pleasure, entertainment, endless scrolling, secret addictions, or relationships that promise belonging but leave them more wounded than before.
And some try to feed their souls with religion while keeping Jesus at a distance.
They know the songs.
They know the language.
They know when to raise their hands.
They know how to appear spiritually strong.
But in private, their hearts are starving.
They are surrounded by Christian content while neglecting prayer.
They can quote Scripture but refuse to forgive.
They defend biblical truth online while secretly protecting sins they know they need to confess.
They want God's gifts without surrendering to God's Son.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question in this entire article is not what Israel asked about the manna.
Perhaps it is this:
What are you using to satisfy a hunger that only Jesus Christ can satisfy?
Be honest.
Not for the audience.
Not for the people who think you're strong.
Not for the church members who assume everything is fine.
Before God.
What is it?
What is the thing you keep returning to when your heart feels empty?
What is the sin you keep excusing?
What is the wound you've allowed to define your identity?
What is the fear that keeps you from trusting the Lord?
What is the secret you are exhausted from carrying?
There is no need to publish your private sins for strangers to examine.
But there is every reason to bring them honestly before the Savior.
Because Jesus did not come to congratulate people who were already spiritually full.
He came to save those who desperately needed mercy.
And the Gospel is not a message that you can repair yourself if you simply try harder.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He lived in obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
That is the message Paul summarizes in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And the invitation is not to pretend you have never sinned.
It is to repent and believe the Gospel.
To turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ.
To stop treating His grace as permission to remain unchanged.
And to receive the forgiveness and new life that only He can give.
This is what makes the story of manna so powerful.
God provided for people who were grumbling in the wilderness.
And in Jesus Christ, God has revealed a mercy far greater than the food Israel gathered from the ground.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we fixed every broken part of our lives.
Not after we convinced the world that we were worthy.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
That doesn't make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible in the light of astonishing grace.
It doesn't make holiness irrelevant.
It means holiness becomes the fruit of belonging to Christ, not the price we pay to purchase His love.
And it doesn't mean every consequence of our past disappears overnight.
Some wounds take time to heal.
Some relationships require difficult conversations.
Some habits demand accountability, prayer, perseverance, and serious change.
But no sinner is beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
The person who betrayed someone's trust.
The person who has wasted years running from God.
The believer who has grown cold.
The parent carrying regret.
The young person secretly ashamed of what they've done.
The person who looks successful on the outside but feels spiritually empty.
The one who wonders whether God would still receive them if everyone knew the truth.
Hear the words of Jesus in John 6:37:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out."
That is not a sentimental slogan.
That is a promise from the Savior.
And perhaps those words are the bread your heart has needed today.
Not another excuse.
Not another distraction.
Not another performance.
Christ Himself.
The One who receives those who come to Him.
The One who forgives.
The One who transforms.
The One who remains faithful.
The One who is greater than the wilderness.
But there is another detail about the manna that is easy to miss.
On the sixth day, Israel was instructed to gather twice the usual amount.
Why?
Because the seventh day was a Sabbath of rest.
Unlike the manna ordinarily kept overnight against God's instructions, the portion preserved for the Sabbath did not spoil.
Exodus 16:22–30 records this remarkable distinction.
The same people who were learning to trust God for food were also learning to obey Him in rest.
They didn't have to gather manna every single morning without interruption.
God had made provision for the day when they were commanded not to gather.
The lesson wasn't that work had no value.
It was that their lives were not ultimately sustained by their own frantic activity.
God was teaching them that His commands and His provision belonged together.
And I wonder how many exhausted believers need to remember that.
You've been carrying responsibilities.
Working long hours.
Caring for people.
Trying to hold your family together.
Trying to stay faithful.
Trying not to fall apart.
And somewhere along the way, you've begun acting as though everything depends entirely on you.
You pray, but you cannot stop worrying.
You worship, but you cannot stop striving.
You say God is in control, but your heart lives as though He has abandoned His throne.
Perhaps today is an invitation to remember that you are a creature, not the Creator.
You are called to faithfulness, not omnipotence.
You are called to obey God, not to become God.
You may need to work diligently.
You may need to make difficult decisions.
You may need to seek wise counsel, accept help, or take practical steps toward resolving a crisis.
But you do not need to carry the illusion that you are the source of your own existence.
Every breath is a gift.
Every mercy is undeserved.
Every day is another opportunity to trust the Lord.
And there is one final wilderness detail that deserves our attention.
Exodus 16:35 tells us that the Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to the border of Canaan.
Forty years.
Not one spectacular morning.
Not one unforgettable week.
Forty years of God's sustaining provision.
Consider the significance.
Children were born into a world where manna was part of ordinary life.
A generation grew up receiving what their parents had once stared at in astonishment.
What began as an unfamiliar wonder became daily sustenance.
And that raises another uncomfortable question.
Have you become so accustomed to God's mercies that you've stopped noticing them?
The ability to breathe.
A meal on the table.
A person who still loves you.
An opportunity to repent.
A Bible you can open.
A church where you can gather.
Another morning in which the Lord has not withdrawn His invitation to seek Him.
None of these should be treated as proof that life will always be comfortable.
Believers can suffer deeply while remaining beloved by God.
But neither should we allow familiarity to erase gratitude.
The manna was extraordinary when Israel first saw it.
And it was still God's provision when they gathered it years later.
Maybe you've been waiting for something dramatic before you will thank God again.
But perhaps there are mercies you have stopped recognizing because they have been present for so long.
And perhaps the greatest mercy of all has become too familiar in your mind.
Jesus Christ.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His forgiveness.
His call to follow Him.
The astonishing truth that the holy Son of God came into a fallen world to save people who could never save themselves.
Don't let the familiarity of the Gospel rob you of its wonder.
Don't become so accustomed to hearing that Jesus died for sinners that you forget what His sacrifice cost.
Don't become so familiar with the words "God loves you" that you stop trembling at the mercy revealed at Calvary.
And don't confuse knowing about the Bread of Life with personally coming to Him in faith.
You can study manna and remain spiritually hungry.
You can know the Hebrew words and still refuse the Savior.
You can understand the Greek grammar and still resist repentance.
Biblical knowledge is precious.
But knowledge is meant to lead us toward the God who has spoken.
The purpose of studying the Scriptures is not merely to collect fascinating details.
It is to know the Lord more truly, trust Him more deeply, and obey Him more faithfully.
And if this article has exposed something in your heart, don't rush away from that conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what needs to be abandoned.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
You don't have to make yourself worthy before coming to Him.
But you must not mistake His mercy for permission to cling to the sins He calls you to forsake.
Come to Christ.
Not merely for what you hope He will give you.
Come because He is worthy.
Come because He is the Savior.
Come because He is the Bread of Life.
And if you don't know what to say, you can begin with a simple, honest prayer:

"Lord Jesus, I have tried to satisfy my soul with things that cannot give me life. I have doubted You, disobeyed You, and often failed to recognize Your goodness. I confess my sin. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Teach me to trust You, turn from sin, and follow You. Let Your Word become precious to me again. I need more than temporary relief. I need You. Amen."
The words themselves are not a magical formula.
Salvation is not earned by repeating a prayer.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ, and genuine faith turns toward Him in repentance.
And if you already belong to Christ but have been spiritually exhausted, remember that the Savior who calls you to follow Him is not indifferent to your weakness.
He knows the wilderness.
He knows suffering.
He knows what it means to be hungry.
Matthew 4 records that Jesus fasted forty days and forty nights and afterward was hungry.
When tempted to turn stones into bread, He answered with Scripture:
"Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God."
Matthew 4:4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3.
And Deuteronomy 8:3 is itself looking back to God's provision of manna in the wilderness.
Do you see the connection?
Israel was taught through manna that life depends upon God's word.
Jesus, facing temptation in the wilderness, trusted and obeyed the Father's word.
Where Israel repeatedly struggled with unbelief, Jesus remained obedient.
And the obedient Son went all the way to the cross for sinners.
This is why the Christian life is not ultimately a story about our heroic ability to survive.
It is a story about the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
From slavery to deliverance.
From hunger to provision.
From rebellion to mercy.
From sin to repentance.
From the cross to the empty tomb.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing the seriousness of sin.
But by redeeming sinners through His death and resurrection and making them new in Him.
And now I want to ask you something.
When you look back at your own wilderness, what do you see?
Only the prayers that haven't been answered yet?
Only the doors that remain closed?
Only the people who disappointed you?
Only the mistakes you cannot undo?
Or can you begin to recognize moments when God sustained you, even when you didn't understand how you would make it through?
Perhaps there were mornings when you didn't know how you would survive another day.
But you did.
Perhaps someone spoke a word of biblical encouragement when you were close to giving up.
Perhaps the Lord used a difficult season to expose a sin you had been refusing to confront.
Perhaps you were led to seek forgiveness, restore a relationship, or finally surrender something you had been holding back.
Those experiences don't make suffering painless.
And they don't mean every event in our lives can be confidently interpreted as a special message from God.
But they can remind us that the Lord is worthy of trust even when our understanding is limited.
The Israelites looked at the ground and asked:
"What is it?"
Moses pointed them toward the Giver.
And Jesus later pointed beyond the manna to Himself.
That is where this story must lead us.
Not merely to an interesting Hebrew expression.
Not merely to a surprising biblical fact.
But to the living Christ.
Because you can receive every earthly blessing you ever prayed for and still miss the greatest gift God has given.
And that gift is His Son.
If you've read this far, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than leaving a quick reaction.
Be honest about where you are spiritually.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ sustained you through a season you thought would destroy you, share what you're comfortable sharing.
Someone else may be walking through a similar wilderness.
Your testimony may help them remember that their circumstances do not place them beyond God's care.
And if someone comes to mind while you're reading this, don't ignore that opportunity to encourage them.
You never know who may be quietly reading, desperately needing to hear the Gospel.
Return to Exodus 16 and John 6.
Read the passages in their full context.
Let Scripture itself strengthen your understanding.
We want this community to be more than a place where people consume inspirational words.
We want it to be a place where Scripture is opened, Christ is exalted, sin is confronted with truth, grace is proclaimed faithfully, and believers are encouraged to grow as disciples of Jesus.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And this is where I want to extend a personal invitation.
But I want to be very clear about something important.
Christ has already paid the price of our redemption.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, not pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
So if you believe in what Gospel Warrior is doing and have the means to support it, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
Not because your money purchases God's favor.
But because faithful generosity can help make biblical teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
These products are secondary.
The Gospel is central.
Our mission is not to sell you a substitute for discipleship.
It is to keep pointing you toward the Savior and helping make biblical resources available to those who want to know Him more deeply.
Pray for this ministry.
Share Scripture faithfully.
Encourage others to read God's Word.
Help us keep the message of repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and new life in Christ before a world that desperately needs to hear it.
Because the goal is not merely to grow a page.
It is to make Jesus known.
To help believers become rooted in Scripture.
To encourage the weary.
To call the wandering to repentance.
To remind the ashamed that forgiveness is found in Christ.
And to keep proclaiming the Gospel without turning God's grace into something people must purchase.
The manna was given by God.
The Bread of Life came from God.
And salvation is received by grace through faith, not bought through human effort.
Imagine the people standing outside their tents.
Their stomachs empty.
Their hearts uncertain.
Their eyes fixed on something they had never seen.
"What is it?"
They didn't understand what was lying before them.
But God had not forgotten their need.
And centuries later, when Jesus stood before the crowds and declared Himself the Bread of Life, the deeper meaning of heaven's provision became unmistakable.
Israel needed bread to survive the wilderness.
We need Jesus Christ to save us from sin and give us eternal life.
And if you're still trying to fill your soul with everything except Him, perhaps today is the day to stop running.
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes easier.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Today.
Come to Jesus.
Trust His mercy.
Repent of your sins.
Receive His Word.
Follow Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be to walk through a wilderness with an empty stomach.
It would be to spend your entire life surrounded by reminders of God's goodness and still reject the Savior He has given.
They woke up asking, "What is this?"—but the question your soul must answer is, "Who is Jesus to me?"
